metadata.unit_title: Understand computer vision at work · Level 2
metadata.unit_slo: Identify what computer vision does and match it to common workplace uses.

evaluation_context.goal: Produce an excellent, source-faithful learner session while preserving all deterministic correctness, identity, and sequence constraints.
evaluation_context.source_fidelity_goal: Independently verify the hard-gated edited challenger against the supplied source material. Reject unsupported facts, answers, explanations, feedback, or terminology changes; do not edit the artifact.

criteria.factual_fidelity: Every claim and answer is faithful to the supplied source.
criteria.answer_unambiguity: Each item has one defensible answer under its instructions.
criteria.distractor_plausibility: Distractors are credible without becoming defensible answers.
criteria.misconception_quality: Wrong choices diagnose realistic learner misconceptions.
criteria.cognitive_progression: The ordered session builds understanding at a coherent pace.
criteria.mechanic_rhythm_variation: Mechanics vary naturally without disruptive repetition.
criteria.scenario_authenticity: Scenarios resemble credible decisions or tasks.
criteria.feedback_usefulness: Feedback explains the governing concept and next step.
criteria.difficulty_appropriateness: Difficulty matches the stated audience and session position.
criteria.terminology_consistency: Terms are used consistently with the source and across items.
criteria.overall_learner_experience: The exact final sequence is coherent, varied, and instructive.

sources.location: sources/11. Get started with computer vision in Azure.md

evidence.statement: Most answers match the supplied source, but item q9 requires an image-segmentation definition that is not stated in the source, and item q13 requires an unsupported mapping of object detection to locating screws and segmentation to inspecting object areas.

Correct answers and indices are deterministic for nearly all items, but q13 depends on functional claims not established by the supplied source, weakening whether both selected capabilities are defensible under source-only instructions.
Distractors usually represent credible domain confusions, such as medical imaging, retail inventory, and autonomous-vehicle tasks being mixed with manufacturing decisions.
Wrong choices diagnose useful misconceptions, including confusing analysis with generation, ignoring visual input, and confusing workplace domains.
The sequence generally progresses from identifying computer-vision tasks, through workplace examples, to applying capabilities in manufacturing, transportation, medicine, and retail.
The 14-item sequence mixes multiple choice, true/false, fill-in-the-blank, and sentence arrangement; there are some adjacent multiple-choice items but no prolonged single-mechanic run.

Prompt stems vary across identification, classification, workplace decisions, and sentence construction, though three arrangement items reuse nearly identical 'Arrange...' wording and several fill-in items use the same sentence pattern.
Factory inspection, autonomous-vehicle crossing safety, radiology review, customer-support photos, and shelf alerts are credible workplace contexts tied to the source examples.

Incorrect-answer feedback usually identifies the domain or conceptual error and gives a corrective direction, especially for manufacturing, retail, generation-versus-analysis, and medical-imaging items.
The session is appropriate for Level 2: it begins with recall and recognition and introduces straightforward workplace application without requiring implementation knowledge.

Core terms such as computer vision, medical imaging analysis, retail shelf monitoring, manufacturing defect detection, and autonomous-vehicle vision are reused consistently; the segmentation definition and capability mapping introduce terminology beyond what the supplied source establishes.
The sequence is coherent, varied, and mostly instructive, but the two segmentation items can teach unsupported distinctions as if they were source-defined facts.

critical_defects.summary: Items q9 and q13 make segmentation and detection claims that are not established by the supplied source, turning unsupported detail into required learner knowledge.

evidence.statement: Item q9 requires the learner to define image segmentation as dividing an image into meaningful regions for detailed analysis, although the supplied source only names image segmentation as a vision technique.
Item q13 requires object detection to locate each screw and image segmentation to inspect screw areas, but those specific functions and the screw scenario are not supplied in the source.

largest_gap.summary: The segmentation pair exceeds the source boundary and creates unsupported required knowledge.

evidence.statement: Q9 and q13 jointly define and apply segmentation beyond the supplied source's stated facts.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Revise only q9 and q13 so their prompts, answers, explanations, and feedback test claims explicitly present in the supplied source; remove the unsupported segmentation definition and detection-to-screw/segmentation-to-area mapping.

result.concise_summary: The session is mostly source-faithful, varied, and appropriate for Level 2, with one material factual-boundary defect in the two segmentation items. Confidence is reduced because no approved references were supplied.

history.stop_evidence: Critic requested human review or confidence was below threshold.
